It was fabulous being at World of Work at Tobacco Dock last week, and MHR is really to be commended for creating and curating such a spectacular event. Inevitably, I attend many conferences, but this was a standout for me. For instance, Neil Martin's talk from his time as a head of strategy for Formula One teams was an epiphany.

HR and marketing have a great deal in common in that both of them have to wrestle with the complex and often highly contradictory matters of psychology, perception, and behaviour (in a world where most of their colleagues are obsessed with reducing everything to an algorithm).

I also think this was great preparation for a future world which is going to be even more contradictory than the one in which we've cut our teeth. One where we need to understand the value of AI and the value of humanity. One where we need to prepare for a workplace which is a mixture of a library and a pub. One where we have to evaluate individual and collective contributions. One where we have to explore the opportunities offered by remote work without losing the value of close human connection.

The people who manage to square the circle, those who can best resolve the apparent contradictions and create something altogether new, will be the people who own the future.

Oh, and we really do need a new name for HR.

If you could see, properly SEE, what your life could become?

The work becomes the reward.

That's the difference. That's the whole difference.

Find the mission and the discipline takes care of itself.

I pray every single one of you finds that flame.

Namaste.

candidates.text:
It sounds simple to “build relationships with executives,” but it’s super difficult in practice.

Many founders try to game this process and think buyers operate like VCs.

If there’s no interest, it’s tough to generate any interest.

Why would a super busy executive give their time of day to a startup that’s not the hottest thing on the market?

The best investors (probably) have executives at large companies on speed dial. That's why there's a high correlation between great investors and large strategic acquisitions. Also, investors aren't interested in small acquisitions. If you aren't a big acquisition, investors may make a few intros but are unlikely to push.

PE buyers are super slow and change their minds a lot. So do strategic buyers unless there's a strong push.
Bankers don't take on smaller companies (sometimes they throw big acquisition multiples to make you a client and sign exclusivity agreements).

Founders also need to move fast because the market is evolving quite rapidly.

Exit is possible, but not always simple.
